questions.question: Coordination number of Cl$^-$ ion in NaCl structure is
questions.answer:
**(C)** 6

NaCl crystallises in the rock-salt structure: each Na$^+$ is surrounded octahedrally by six Cl$^-$ and each Cl$^-$ by six Na$^+$, so both ions have coordination number 6. The structure is two interpenetrating f.c.c. lattices with 4 formula units per unit cell.

questions.question: $\ce{H2 + Cl2 ->[h\nu] 2HCl}$ (gas) is
questions.answer:
**(B)** zero order reaction

This is a **photochemical** reaction. Its rate depends on the intensity of the light absorbed, not on the concentrations of H$_2$ and Cl$_2$, so the rate law is $\text{rate}=k[\text{Cl}_2]^0[H_2]^0=k$ — zero order. (The chain itself involves Cl atoms, but the overall measured rate is independent of the reactants' concentrations.)

questions.question: The normality of 0.2 (N) aqueous solution of a dibasic acid is
questions.answer:
**(A)** 0.4 N

Normality = molarity × basicity. A dibasic acid furnishes two H$^+$ per molecule, so its equivalent mass is half its molar mass and its normality is twice its molarity:

$$N=0.2\times2=0.4\ \text{N}$$

(Equivalently, $\ce{H2A}$ with $M=0.2$ mol L$^{-1}$ supplies $0.4$ mol of H$^+$ per litre.

questions.question: Which of the following ores is concentrated by the froth floatation process?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Copper pyrite

Froth floatation is used for **sulphide** ores. Powdered copper pyrite (CuFeS$_2$) is wetted by oil rather than water, so on blowing air it clings to the bubbles and rises as a froth, while the siliceous gangue sinks. Hematite, magnetite and bauxite are oxide ores and are concentrated by magnetic separation or leaching.

questions.question: The value of colligative properties of a solution increases when solute molecules undergo
questions.answer:
**(B)** dissociation

Colligative properties count particles. Ionisation increases the number of particles above the number of formula units, so the effect is larger than expected and $i>1$ — e.g. NaCl gives two ions. Association (dimerisation) halves the particle count and *lowers* the effect, giving $i<1$.

questions.question: When NH$_3$ is reacted with excess of alkyl halide, we get
questions.answer:
**(D)** a mixture of all these

The substitution proceeds stepwise and each product is still nucleophilic:

$$\ce{NH3 ->[RX] RNH2 ->[RX] R2NH ->[RX] R3N ->[RX] R4N^+X^-}$$

With excess alkyl halide the reaction is carried right through, so primary, secondary and tertiary amines plus the quaternary salt are all present. Excess ammonia is used when the primary amine is wanted.

questions.question: C$_2$H$_5$Cl on heating with alcoholic KOH will produce
questions.answer:
**(B)** C$_2$H$_4$

Alcoholic KOH is a base, not a nucleophile in this medium, and eliminates HCl:

$$\ce{CH3CH2Cl + KOH(alc) -> CH2=CH2 + KCl + H2O}$$

The product is ethene; aqueous KOH would give ethanol by substitution.

questions.question: Oxidation number of Mn in MnO$_4^-$ is
questions.answer:
**(D)** 7

Let Mn be $x$ and each O be −2:

$$x+4(-2)=-1\ \Rightarrow\ x=+7$$

Manganese is therefore in its highest state, +7, in permanganate — a $d^0$ ion, colourless in itself, the deep purple colour arising from a charge-transfer transition.

questions.question: Define parts per million (ppm).
questions.answer:
**Parts per million (ppm)** is a way of expressing very small concentrations: the number of parts by mass of one component per million parts by mass of the solution (for gases, by volume):

$$\text{ppm}=\frac{\text{parts of the component}}{\text{parts of solution}}\times10^{6}$$

It is used for traces — dissolved oxygen in water, pollutants in air, or impurities in a sample: 1 ppm means 1 g of solute in $10^{6}$ g of solution, i.e. 1 mg per kg.

questions.question: Write the I.U.P.A.C. name of $\ce{CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)-CO-CH3}$ and $\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3}$.
questions.answer:
**(i) $\ce{CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)-CO-CH3}$** — the longest chain containing the carbonyl carbon has five carbons, numbered from the ketone end so the carbonyl is C-2; the methyl branch then sits on C-3:

**3-methylpentan-2-one**

**(ii) $\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3}$** — a straight five-carbon ketone with the carbonyl at C-2:

**pentan-2-one** (trivial name: methyl propyl ketone)

questions.question: Write an isomer of acetic acid.
questions.answer:
**Methyl formate, $\ce{HCOOCH3}$** — an ester with the same molecular formula $\ce{C2H4O2}$ but a different functional group (an ester rather than a carboxylic acid), so it is a functional isomer.

*(Also acceptable: the hydroxy-aldehyde $\ce{HOCH2CHO}$, glycolaldehyde, and ethylene glycol's cyclic peroxide — but methyl formate is the standard answer.)* Acetic acid itself is $\ce{CH3COOH}$; isomerism between a carboxylic acid and an ester of the same formula is very common in this series.

questions.question: What is order of reaction?
questions.answer:
**The order of a reaction** is the sum of the powers (coefficients) of the concentration terms in the experimentally determined rate law. For

$$\text{rate}=k[A]^{x}[B]^{y}$$

the order is $x+y$ with respect to A and B; the order with respect to A alone is $x$. It can be zero, integral or fractional, and is found by experiment, not from the balanced equation. For the first-order reaction $\ce{A -> P}$, rate $=k[A]$ and the order is 1.

questions.question: Name a hypnotic drug.
questions.answer:
**Benzodiazepine** — for example **diazepam (Valium)**; other hypnotics are the barbiturates such as **Veronal (barbital)**, **Luminal (phenobarbital)** and **Seconal**.

Hypnotics are central-nervous-system depressants that induce sleep; in smaller doses the same drugs act as sedatives or tranquillisers.

questions.question: Write the structural formula of aspirin.
questions.answer:
**Aspirin** is **acetylsalicylic acid** — a benzene ring bearing a carboxyl group at C-1 and an acetoxy group, $\ce{-OCOCH3}$, at C-2 (ortho):

$$\ce{2-CH3COO-C6H4-COOH}$$

Structure: benzene ring with $\ce{-COOH}$ and $\ce{-OCOCH3}$ on adjacent carbons. It is made by acetylating salicylic acid with acetic anhydride:

$$\ce{C6H4(OH)(COOH) + (CH3CO)2O -> C6H4(OCOCH3)(COOH) + CH3COOH}$$

Aspirin is an analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory drug, and also reduces platelet aggregation.

questions.question: Complete the following reaction: $\ce{C6H5COOH + NaOH ->[CaO][\Delta]}$
questions.answer:
This is **decarboxylation** by heating the sodium salt with soda lime (NaOH/CaO):

$$\ce{C6H5COOH + NaOH -> C6H5COONa + H2O}$$

$$\ce{C6H5COONa + NaOH ->[CaO][\Delta] C6H6 + Na2CO3}$$

The product is **benzene**. Soda lime is used because it is less corrosive than NaOH alone and keeps the mixture friable; the overall change is the loss of CO$_2$ from the acid, which is why the reaction is the standard laboratory preparation of benzene from benzoic acid.

questions.question: Write any two features that distinguish between physisorption and chemisorption.
questions.answer:
| Physisorption | Chemisorption |
|---|---|
| Weak van der Waals forces | Strong, chemical-bond forces |
| Low heat of adsorption, 20–40 kJ/mol | High heat of adsorption, 80–240 kJ/mol |
| Occurs at low temperature; reversible; multilayer | Occurs at high temperature; irreversible; monolayer only |
| Not specific, and needs no activation energy | Highly specific, and requires an activation energy |

*Any two contrasted pairs.* The extent of physisorption correlates with the ease of liquefaction of the gas, whereas chemisorption does not.

questions.question: Complete the following: (i) $\ce{NaBr + H2SO4 ->[MnO2][\Delta]}$ (ii) $\ce{I2 + Na2S2O3}$
questions.answer:
**(i)** Sodium bromide with concentrated sulphuric acid and manganese dioxide on heating gives bromine — the laboratory preparation of bromine, with MnO$_2$ oxidising the HBr formed *in situ*:

$$\ce{2NaBr + MnO2 + 3H2SO4 ->[\Delta] 2NaHSO4 + MnSO4 + Br2 + 2SO2 + 2H2O}$$

The bromine distils over as red-brown vapours.

**(ii)** Iodine is reduced by thiosulphate, which is oxidised to tetrathionate:

$$\ce{I2 + 2Na2S2O3 -> 2NaI + Na2S4O6}$$

This is the iodometric titration reaction; the brown colour of iodine disappears at the end point.

questions.question: What is the difference between roasting and calcination?
questions.answer:
| Roasting | Calcination |
|---|---|
| Carried out in the **presence of excess air** | Carried out in the **absence or limited supply of air** |
| A sulphide ore is converted to the oxide | A carbonate or hydrated oxide ore is converted to the oxide |
| An oxidation process: $\ce{2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2}$ | A thermal decomposition: $\ce{ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2}$ |
| Generally at a higher temperature | Just below the melting point of the ore |

Both steps are used to convert an ore to the oxide from which the metal is then reduced. (Note the printed key has the two columns' equations interchanged — the table above is the correct assignment.)

questions.question: What are transition elements? Zn is not a transition element. Why?
questions.answer:
**Transition elements** are the d-block elements whose atoms or ions have an incompletely filled d subshell in the ground state or in one of their common oxidation states; their general electronic configuration is $(n-1)d^{1-9}ns^{1-2}$.

**Why zinc is not one:** zinc has the configuration $3d^{10}4s^{2}$ — a **completely filled** d subshell — and its only common oxidation state, +2, also gives $3d^{10}$. With no partially filled d orbitals it can show neither $d$–$d$ transitions (so its compounds are colourless) nor the variable valency, paramagnetism and catalytic behaviour typical of transition metals. Zinc is therefore treated as a d-block element but not a transition element.

questions.question: Write any two differences between CH$_3$OH and C$_2$H$_5$OH.
questions.answer:
| Property | CH$_3$OH (methyl alcohol) | C$_2$H$_5$OH (ethyl alcohol) |
|---|---|---|
| Heating with iodine and alkali | No iodoform is formed (no $\ce{CH3CH(OH)-}$ group) | Yellow crystals of iodoform are formed, with a characteristic smell |
| Heating with bleaching powder | No chloroform is formed | Chloroform is formed, recognised by its sweet smell |
| Warming with concentrated H$_2$SO$_4$ | Pungent smell of formaldehyde (from oxidation) | Sweet smell of acetaldehyde |

The iodoform test is the standard practical distinction between the two alcohols.

questions.question: Write about aluminothermic process with two examples.
questions.answer:
In the **aluminothermic (thermite) process** a metal oxide that carbon cannot reduce satisfactorily is heated with aluminium powder. Aluminium's very high affinity for oxygen makes the reduction strongly exothermic, and the metal is obtained molten:

$$\ce{Cr2O3 + 2Al -> 2Cr + Al2O3}$$

$$\ce{Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3}$$

The second reaction is the thermite reaction used to weld railway tracks, reaching about 3000 °C. The method is used for metals of high melting point such as chromium and manganese. Some activation energy is always needed, so the mixture must be ignited (with a magnesium ribbon fuse), but once started it is self-sustaining.

questions.question: What is natural rubber? Write down the name and structural formula of its monomer.
questions.answer:
**Natural rubber** is a linear, elastic polymer of isoprene obtained as latex from the rubber tree; it is cis-1,4-polyisoprene.

**Monomer:** **isoprene — 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene**, $\ce{CH2=C(CH3)-CH=CH2}$.

The polymer chain is

$$\ce{[-CH2-C(CH3)=CH-CH2-]_n}$$

with the double bond in the *cis* configuration, which is what makes the chains coil and gives rubber its elasticity. Vulcanisation with sulphur cross-links the chains and hardens the product.

questions.question: What happens when phenol reacts with (a) NaOH (b) dil. HNO$_3$?
questions.answer:
**(a) With NaOH:** phenol, being weakly acidic, dissolves in alkali to give **sodium phenoxide**:

$$\ce{C6H5OH + NaOH -> C6H5ONa + H2O}$$

The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance, which is why phenol (pK$_a$ ≈ 10) is much more acidic than an alcohol (pK$_a$ ≈ 16).

**(b) With dilute HNO$_3$ at 293 K:** nitration takes place at the ortho and para positions, giving a mixture of **o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol**:

$$\ce{C6H5OH + HNO3(dil) ->[293 K] o-HOC6H4NO2 + p-HOC6H4NO2 + H2O}$$

The —OH group is activating and ortho/para directing; with concentrated acid, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid) is obtained.

questions.question: Describe any three factors which affect the rate of chemical reaction.
questions.answer:
**1. Concentration.** At a given temperature the rate depends on the concentration of one or more reactants (and sometimes of the products, in a reversible reaction); a higher concentration means more collisions per second, so a higher rate. In a heterogeneous reaction the *surface area* of the solid plays the same role — powdered calcium carbonate reacts far faster with acid than a single lump.

**2. Temperature.** The rate rises steeply with temperature — roughly doubling or tripling for each 10 K — mainly because the fraction of molecules with energy above the activation energy grows exponentially, $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$.

**3. Presence of a catalyst (or of light).** A catalyst provides a path of lower activation energy and so accelerates the reaction without being consumed. Photochemical reactions such as $\ce{H2 + Cl2 ->[h\nu] 2HCl}$ take place only in the presence of light, and their rate depends on the intensity of the radiation absorbed.

questions.question: Explain the difference between globular and fibrous proteins.
questions.answer:
**Globular proteins** are those in which the polypeptide chain is coiled into a compact, roughly spherical shape held by hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and hydrophobic effects. They are generally **soluble in water** and are the working molecules of the cell — almost all enzymes, hormones and transport proteins are globular. Examples: **insulin, albumins, haemoglobin**.

**Fibrous proteins** consist of polypeptide chains arranged side by side in long threads or sheets, held together by hydrogen bonds and **disulphide bridges between chains**. They are **insoluble in water**, are mechanically strong and play a structural (or contractile) role in the organism. Examples: **collagen, myosin, keratin** (hair, wool, nails).

So the difference is both one of shape and of function: globular proteins are soluble functional molecules, fibrous proteins insoluble structural ones.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following conversions? (i) Propene → Propan-2-ol (ii) Ethyl magnesium bromide → 2-methylpropan-2-ol (iii) Benzyl chloride → Benzyl alcohol
questions.answer:
(i) **Propene → propan-2-ol:** acid-catalysed hydration obeys Markovnikov's rule, so the OH goes to the middle carbon:

$$\ce{CH3-CH=CH2 + H2O ->[H2SO4] CH3-CH(OH)-CH3}$$

(ii) **Ethyl magnesium bromide → 2-methylpropan-2-ol:** the Grignard reagent adds across the carbonyl of propanone, and the alkoxide is hydrolysed:

$$\ce{(CH3)2C=O + C2H5MgBr -> (CH3)2(C2H5)C-OMgBr ->[H2O] (CH3)2(C2H5)C-OH}$$ 

A tertiary alcohol with four carbon atoms in the main chain results because the carbonyl carbon already carries two methyl groups.

(iii) **Benzyl chloride → benzyl alcohol:** hydrolysis with aqueous alkali, by the S$_N$1 route (the benzylic cation is stabilised by the aromatic ring):

$$\ce{C6H5CH2Cl + KOH(aq) -> C6H5CH2OH + KCl}$$

Even moist silver oxide or boiling water will bring it about, which shows how reactive a benzylic halide is.

questions.question: Describe the contact process for the manufacture of sulphuric acid.
questions.answer:
**Contact process** — the industrial manufacture of H$_2$SO$_4$.

**Step 1 — sulphur dioxide.** Sulphur is burned in air (or sulphide ores roasted):

$$\ce{S + O2 -> SO2}$$

**Step 2 — catalytic oxidation to sulphur trioxide.** This is the reversible, exothermic heart of the process, carried out over $\ce{V2O5}$:

$$\ce{2SO2 + O2 <=>[V2O5] 2SO3},\qquad \Delta H=-197\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

By Le Chatelier's principle the yield of SO$_3$ is favoured by **low temperature and high pressure**, but the rate would then be impractically slow and the cost too high, so the **optimum conditions** are a compromise: about **700 K** (720–750 K) and **2 atm**, with a slight excess of oxygen and repeated passes over the catalyst. A promoted vanadium(V) oxide, with K$_2$O and Al$_2$O$_3$, lowers the activation energy and speeds the reaction.

**Step 3 — absorption and dilution.** SO$_3$ is absorbed in concentrated H$_2$SO$_4$ (not in water, which gives an unrecoverable acid mist) forming oleum, which is then diluted:

$$\ce{SO3 + H2SO4 -> H2S2O7}$$

$$\ce{H2S2O7 + H2O -> 2H2SO4}$$

questions.question: Complete the following: (i) $\ce{C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + KOH ->}$ (ii) $\ce{C6H5N2Cl + C2H5OH ->}$ (iii) $\ce{C6H5NH2 + HNO2 ->}$
questions.answer:
(i) **Carbylamine reaction** (test for primary amines):

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH -> C6H5NC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

**Phenyl isocyanide** is formed, with an unbearable smell.

(ii) **Reduction of the diazonium salt by ethanol:**

$$\ce{C6H5N2Cl + C2H5OH -> C6H6 + N2 + CH3CHO + HCl}$$

**Benzene** is obtained (ethanol is oxidised to acetaldehyde).

(iii) **Diazotisation** at 273–278 K:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + HNO2 + HCl ->[273-278 K] C6H5N2^+Cl^- + 2H2O}$$

**Benzene diazonium chloride**; on warming this decomposes to phenol.

questions.question: Determine the oxidation states of the central metal ion in the following complex compounds: (a) K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$] (b) [Cr(H$_2$O)$_6$]Cl$_3$ (c) [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]Cl$_3$
questions.answer:
**(a) K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$]:** the anion carries −4, with six CN$^-$ at −1 each:

$$x+6(-1)=-4\ \Rightarrow\ x=+2$$

**Fe is +2** (ferrocyanide). (The printed key's answer of +2 is right; the intermediate line printed in the book is garbled.)

**(b) [Cr(H$_2$O)$_6$]Cl$_3$:** the cation carries +3 and H$_2$O is neutral:

$$x+6(0)=+3\ \Rightarrow\ x=+3$$

**Cr is +3**.

**(c) [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]Cl$_3$:** likewise

$$x+6(0)=+3\ \Rightarrow\ x=+3$$

**Co is +3**.

In each case the sum of the ligand charges plus the metal's oxidation state equals the overall charge on the complex ion.

questions.question: What are the differences between DNA and RNA?
questions.answer:
| RNA (ribonucleic acid) | DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) |
|---|---|
| The sugar is **D-ribose** | The sugar is **2-deoxy-D-ribose** (one OH less) |
| Contains the bases **cytosine, uracil, guanine, adenine** — uracil replaces thymine | Contains **cytosine, thymine, guanine, adenine** — no uracil |
| A **single** strand of polynucleotides (though it can fold) | A **double** helix of two polynucleotide chains held by base pairing |
| Formed from DNA; cannot replicate itself | Can replicate itself (semi-conservative replication) |
| Present in both nucleus and cytoplasm; carries out protein synthesis | Present mainly in the nucleus; stores and transmits the genetic information |

Both are polymers of nucleotides, each nucleotide being a base + sugar + phosphate group.

questions.question: Complete the following reactions: (i) $\ce{CH3CHO + NH2OH ->}$ (ii) $\ce{C6H5NH2 + Br2(aq) ->}$
questions.answer:
(i) Acetaldehyde with hydroxylamine gives **acetaldehyde oxime**:

$$\ce{CH3CHO + NH2OH -> CH3CH=NOH + H2O}$$

(nucleophilic addition of the nitrogen to the carbonyl carbon, then elimination of water).

(ii) Aniline with bromine water gives an immediate **white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline**:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + 3Br2(aq) -> 2,4,6-Br3C6H2NH2 v + 3HBr}$$

The —NH$_2$ group activates the ring so strongly that no Lewis-acid catalyst is required; this is the standard test for aniline.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following transformations? (i) Acetic acid into acetone (ii) Acetaldehyde into lactic acid (iii) Acetone to iodoform (iv) Propanone to propene (v) Benzoic acid to m-nitrobenzyl alcohol
questions.answer:
(i) **Acetic acid → acetone:** the calcium salt is dry-distilled:

$$\ce{2CH3COOH ->[Ca(OH)2] (CH3COO)2Ca ->[\Delta] CH3COCH3 + CaCO3}$$

(ii) **Acetaldehyde → lactic acid:** hydrogen cyanide adds to the carbonyl, and the cyanohydrin is hydrolysed:

$$\ce{CH3CHO + HCN -> CH3CH(OH)CN ->[H2O/H^+] CH3CH(OH)COOH}$$

(iii) **Acetone → iodoform:** heating with iodine and alkali:

$$\ce{CH3COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> CHI3 v + CH3COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O}$$

(iv) **Propanone → propene:** reduction to propan-2-ol, then dehydration:

$$\ce{CH3COCH3 ->[LiAlH4][\text{or NaBH4}] CH3CH(OH)CH3 ->[\text{conc. }H2SO4][443 K] CH3CH=CH2}$$

(v) **Benzoic acid → m-nitrobenzyl alcohol:** nitration (the —COOH group is meta directing) followed by reduction of the carboxyl group to the alcohol:

$$\ce{C6H5COOH ->[HNO3][H2SO4] m-NO2C6H4COOH ->[LiAlH4] m-NO2C6H4CH2OH}$$

*Distinguish:* **propanal and propanone** by Tollens' or Fehling's test — propanal, being an aldehyde, gives a silver mirror and a red precipitate of Cu$_2$O, while propanone does not. **Phenol and benzoic acid** by the neutral FeCl$_3$ test — phenol gives a violet colour (an iron–phenoxide complex), benzoic acid gives no colour; benzoic acid also effervesces with NaHCO$_3$, phenol does not.

questions.question: What are inter-halogen compounds? Give two examples. What are Freons? Give two examples. / The half-life period of a first order reaction is 100 minutes. Calculate the time required for the reaction to be completed by 90%.
questions.answer:
**(a) Inter-halogen compounds** are compounds containing only two or more different halogens bonded to each other, generally of the form XY, XY$_3$, XY$_5$ or XY$_7$ where X is the larger, less electronegative halogen. Examples: **iodine monobromide, IBr**, and **chlorine trifluoride, $\ce{ClF3}$**. They are covalent, and their formation shows that halogens can act towards one another as electropositive and electronegative partners.

**(b) Freons** are chlorofluorocarbons (fluorochlorohydrocarbons) used as refrigerants, propellants and in air-conditioning because they are non-toxic and chemically inert: **Freon-12, $\ce{CF2Cl2}$**, and **Freon-11, $\ce{CFCl3}$**. Their escape into the atmosphere has been restricted because they release chlorine atoms that destroy stratospheric ozone.

**Numerical.** For a first-order reaction, with $t_{1/2}=100$ min:

$$k=\frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{0.693}{100}=6.93\times10^{-3}\ \text{min}^{-1}$$

For 90% completion, $[R]=0.1[R]_0$:

$$t=\frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{[R]_0}{[R]}=\frac{2.303}{6.93\times10^{-3}}\log\frac{100}{10}$$

$$=\frac{2.303}{6.93\times10^{-3}}\times1=\frac{2.303}{0.00693}=332.3\ \text{min}$$

**The reaction takes about 332 minutes** (3.32 half-lives) to be 90% complete. (The printed key works the same problem with $k=0.0693$ and gets the same 332.3 min.)

questions.question: (a) State Faraday's laws of electrolysis. (b) How much copper will be deposited at cathode of an electrolytic cell containing Cu$^{2+}$ ion by the passage of 2 ampere current for 60 minutes?
questions.answer:
**(a) Faraday's laws of electrolysis.**

**First law:** the mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed:

$$w\propto Q\ \Rightarrow\ w=ZQ=ZIt$$

where $Z$ is the electrochemical equivalent — the mass deposited by one coulomb. Since 96500 C (1 faraday) deposits one gram equivalent, $Z=E/96500$.

**Second law:** when the same quantity of charge is passed through different electrolytes in series, the masses deposited at the electrodes are proportional to their chemical equivalent masses:

$$\frac{w_1}{w_2}=\frac{E_1}{E_2}\qquad\text{or}\qquad \frac{w_1}{E_1}=\frac{w_2}{E_2}=\frac{Q}{96500}$$

**(b) Copper deposited.** At the cathode $\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- -> Cu}$, so 2 faraday give 1 mole of copper, i.e. 63.5 g.

Number of faradays passed:

$$F=\frac{It}{96500}=\frac{2\times60\times60}{96500}=\frac{7200}{96500}=0.0746\ \text{F}$$

Mass deposited:

$$w=0.0746\times\frac{63.5}{2}=0.0746\times31.75=2.37\ \text{g}$$

(Equivalently $w=\dfrac{2\times3600\times31.75}{96500}=2.37$ g.) **About 2.37 g of copper** is deposited. Note that the equivalent mass of copper is 31.75 g eq$^{-1}$, not 63.5, because Cu$^{2+}$ needs two electrons per ion.

questions.question: (a) Write the principle for the production of NH$_3$ in Haber's process. (b) What happens when NH$_3$ reacts with (i) Na (ii) CO$_2$?
questions.answer:
**(a) Haber's process.** Nitrogen and hydrogen are combined directly:

$$\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)},\qquad \Delta H=-92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

The reaction is reversible, exothermic and accompanied by a decrease in the number of gas moles. By Le Chatelier's principle the **forward** reaction is favoured by **low temperature and high pressure**. In practice a compromise is needed because the rate is negligible at low temperature, so the process runs at about **700 K (723 K)** and **200 atm**, with a **finely divided iron catalyst** promoted by K$_2$O, Al$_2$O$_3$ and some oxides of calcium — the promoter increases the activity and life of the catalyst; the mixture is also recycled, with ammonia condensed out.

**(b) (i) With sodium** at about 575 K, ammonia loses a proton and gives sodium amide, hydrogen being evolved:

$$\ce{2NH3(l) + 2Na(s) -> 2NaNH2 + H2}$$ 

**(ii) With carbon dioxide** at 453–475 K and 220 atm, ammonium carbamate is formed, which dehydrates to urea:

$$\ce{2NH3 + CO2 -> NH2COONH4 -> NH2CONH2 + H2O}$$

This is the industrial manufacture of urea fertiliser.
